issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may set aside an acquittal when the acquittal rests on an erroneous or perverse assessment of the evidence, but must not disturb it when two reasonable views are possible.
material_facts: The High Court acquitted the accused after reversing the trial court’s convictions.
The Supreme Court found that the High Court had ignored material evidence and relied on flimsy and untenable reasons, while the eyewitness and corroborative evidence supported the prosecution case.
issues.conclusion: The acquittal was set aside and the trial court’s convictions were restored, with the sentences modified as to the death penalty and default imprisonment.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sambasivan v. State of Kerala and Chandrappa v. State of Karnataka, an appellate court may fully review and reassess the evidence in an appeal against acquittal. The accused retain a double presumption of innocence, and an acquittal should not be disturbed if two reasonable conclusions are possible; interference is warranted where the acquittal reflects an erroneous approach to the evidence or conclusions that are perverse. The Supreme Court exercised its appellate jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The challenged appellate judgment acquitted persons who had been convicted at trial.
predicates.material_evidence_supports_prosecution: The record contained eyewitness and corroborative evidence supporting the prosecution account.
predicates.acquittal_based_on_perverse_or_erroneous: The acquitting court disregarded relevant evidence or reached conclusions unsupported by a proper assessment of the record.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an acquittal, material evidence supports the prosecution, and the acquittal rests on a perverse or erroneous assessment, the appellate court may set it aside.

issues.legal_issue: Minor discrepancies in eyewitness testimony and medical evidence that does not rule out the eyewitness account do not require that account to be rejected.
material_facts: The principal eyewitness’s evidence was recorded over a prolonged period in several stages, and the court found his account consistent on material matters.
A second eyewitness fairly corroborated that account.

The doctor stated in examination-in-chief that the incident could have occurred at the time described by the eyewitness, and the absence of blunt injuries did not make the eyewitness account impossible.
Physical evidence, including bloodstained clay and cartridges, and witness testimony supported the stated place of occurrence.
issues.conclusion: The eyewitness evidence was reliable and the High Court should not have rejected it based on minor discrepancies, medical evidence that did not exclude the account, or its assessment of the place and timing of the incident.
issues.legal_principle: In Darbara Singh v. State of Punjab, the Court held that oral evidence ordinarily has primacy unless it is totally irreconcilable with medical evidence; medical evidence warrants rejection of ocular testimony only when it completely rules out the possibility that the testimony is true. Minor discrepancies, particularly where evidence was recorded after delay or in a piecemeal manner, do not by themselves make otherwise consistent and corroborated eyewitness evidence unreliable.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and eyewitness_account_consistent_on_material_facts and eyewitness_account_corroborated and medical_evidence_does_not_exclude_account

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The challenged appellate judgment acquitted persons who had been convicted at trial.
predicates.eyewitness_account_consistent_on_materia: An eyewitness gave an account that remained consistent on material matters despite minor discrepancies in testimony recorded over time.
predicates.eyewitness_account_corroborated: Another witness or physical evidence supported material parts of the eyewitness account.
predicates.medical_evidence_does_not_exclude_accoun: The medical evidence did not make the eyewitness account impossible or rule out its truth.

issues.definition: In an appeal against acquittal, a materially consistent and corroborated eyewitness account is not rejected for minor discrepancies when the medical evidence does not exclude it.

issues.legal_issue: The prosecution is not defeated merely because an injured witness could not be examined after being threatened and abducted, or because no independent witness was produced, where other eyewitness evidence is trustworthy.
material_facts: The prosecution attempted to produce an injured witness but could not do so after he was threatened and abducted during the relevant period, as supported by reports made to the police.
The prosecution did not produce an independent witness.
The court found the evidence of the two eyewitnesses trustworthy.
issues.conclusion: The injured witness’s non-examination was not fatal, no adverse inference was warranted on that basis, and the absence of an independent witness alone did not justify doubting the prosecution case.
issues.legal_principle: Under Rajan Rai v. State of Bihar, non-examination of an injured witness does not require an adverse inference where the prosecution’s inability to produce the witness is explained. The absence of independent witnesses is not by itself a ground to reject a prosecution case when the eyewitness evidence is trustworthy.

rule.if: criminal_trial and injured_witness_unavailable_after_threats_or_abduction and reliable_eyewitness_evidence and no_independent_witness_produced

predicates.criminal_trial: The matter is a criminal prosecution in which the prosecution presents witnesses to prove the alleged offence.
predicates.injured_witness_unavailable_after_threat: An injured witness could not be produced after being threatened or abducted during the relevant proceedings.
predicates.reliable_eyewitness_evidence: Other eyewitness testimony was found trustworthy.
predicates.no_independent_witness_produced: The prosecution did not produce a witness independent of the parties.

issues.definition: In a criminal trial, an injured witness’s explained unavailability and the absence of independent witnesses do not defeat the prosecution when other eyewitness evidence is trustworthy.

issues.legal_issue: A documented prior dispute may support the prosecution’s account of motive, while an alibi is not established when the accused fail to provide cogent evidence supporting their claimed absence.
material_facts: The complainant described a land dispute between the parties and had made complaints about it before the incident.
The accused who relied on alibis did not produce cogent evidence establishing that they were elsewhere at the relevant time.
issues.conclusion: The court accepted that the prior dispute supported the prosecution’s claim of motive and held that the accused had failed to establish their alibis.
issues.legal_principle: The court treated the prior dispute and contemporaneous complaints as evidence supporting motive and assessed the alibi pleas against the evidence offered in support of them. It relied on no earlier case or specific statutory provision for this determination.

rule.if: criminal_prosecution and prior_dispute_supported_by_documented_complaints and accused_assert_alibi and alibi_lacks_cogent_support

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The matter is a criminal prosecution concerning an alleged offence.
predicates.prior_dispute_supported_by_documented_co: The complainant described a pre-existing dispute and had made documented complaints about it before the alleged offence.
predicates.accused_assert_alibi: One or more accused claimed that they were elsewhere when the alleged offence occurred.
predicates.alibi_lacks_cogent_support: The accused did not produce cogent evidence supporting their claimed absence.

issues.definition: In a criminal prosecution, documented complaints supporting a prior dispute and an alibi unsupported by cogent evidence support a finding of motive and a finding that the alibi was not established.

issues.legal_issue: A death sentence is not justified when the circumstances do not establish that the case is among the rarest of rare cases.
material_facts: The trial court imposed death sentences on two accused persons.
The Supreme Court was not persuaded that the reasoning or circumstances established that the case warranted the death penalty.
issues.conclusion: The death sentences were replaced with sentences of life imprisonment.
issues.legal_principle: The death penalty is reserved for the rarest of rare cases. The Court applied that principle in reviewing the trial court’s sentence and concluded that the case did not meet that threshold; no earlier case or specific statutory provision was cited for this sentencing determination.

predicates.criminal_appeal_involving_death_sentence: The matter is a criminal appeal in which a death sentence is under review.
predicates.lower_court_imposed_death_sentence: A lower court imposed the death penalty on the accused.
predicates.circumstances_do_not_meet_rarest_case_th: The circumstances and reasons on the record do not establish that the case warrants the most exceptional punishment.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal, a death sentence is replaced with life imprisonment when the lower court imposed death but the circumstances do not meet the highest exceptional threshold.
